{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=mechanisms+for+autonomous+identification+and+falsification+of+foundational+reasoning+assumptions+in+AI+agents&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6759126\", \"title\": [\"An Engineering Framework for Self-Correcting Autonomous AI Agents: Mitigating Hallucinations and Reasoning Loops in Autonomous Engineering Workflows\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>This paper presents TRACE (Trajectory Reliability and Correction Engine), a runtime self-correction framework for autonomous AI agents in engineering workflows. TRACE targets a reliability gap in multi-step tool-using agents, where unsupported claims, contradictions, repetitive loops, and tool-use anomalies can propagate across long execution trajectories. Existing self-correction methods typically rely on post-hoc reflection or a single intervention mechanism, but do not integrate continuous runtime monitoring, failure attribution, and adaptive recovery in one control layer. TRACE wraps a standard ReAct-style agent with four modules: a Trajectory Monitor, a Failure Attribution module, a Recovery Controller, and an Audit Layer for structured trace logging. We evaluate TRACE on a simulated enterprise incident-triage benchmark of 50 tasks with injected hallucination- and loop-inducing conditions across four difficulty levels. TRACE achieves 76.0% task success versus 68.0% for a self-reflection baseline and 62.0% for vanilla ReAct, while reducing hallucination incidence from 19.4% to 9.6% and loop frequency from 12.1% to 4.8%. The framework is intended for reliable, auditable autonomous execution in engineering environments.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6759126\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/lmxo2289\", \"title\": [\"Reasoning under compliance assumptions in normative multiagent systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The use of norms in multiagent systems has proven to be a successful approach in order to coordinate and regulate the behaviour of participating agents. In such normative systems it is generally assumed that agents can obey or disobey norms. In this paper, we develop a logical framework for normative systems that allows reasoning about agents' abilities under a multitude of norm compliance assumptions. In particular, we investigate different types of norm compliance and propose an extension of Alternating Temporal Logic (ATL) to reason about the abilities of (coalitions of) agents under different types of norm compliance assumptions. For this extension we show that the problem of model-checking remains close to the domain of standard ATL. Finally, we show that some norms can limit an agent's autonomy in the sense that an agent cannot control the violation of these norms. We present and discuss various classes of the so-called self-supporting norms, i.e., norms for which individual agents have control over their violations.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/lmxo2289\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2012, 6, 4]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.65109/gmqn5969\", \"title\": [\"The role of assumption identification in autonomous agent reasoning\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The concept of autonomy is central to the notion of agenthood and has been addressed by many researchers in the multi-agent systems community. We argue that the degree to which an agent's reasoning is autonomous is affected by the degree to which it is able to choose its assumptions autonomously. We discuss a technique that enables agents to identify appropriate assumptions dynamically, by employing representations of norms in Default Logic.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.65109/gmqn5969\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2009, 5, 10]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6956178\", \"title\": [\"Cognitive Internet Layer (CIL): The Foundational Trust and Reasoning Infrastructure for Autonomous Intelligence Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The current internet architecture was fundamentally designed for deterministic data packet transport and applicationlevel request-response interactions, not for the semantic exchange, verification, governance, and replay of autonomous machine reasoning. As autonomous AI agents scale globally to orchestrate critical infrastructure, medical networks, corporate supply chains, and legal workflows, traditional integration patterns create structural bottlenecks. These limitations introduce severe risks of cognitive fragmentation, black-box opacity, and cascade errors across organizational boundaries. This paper proposes the Cognitive Internet Layer (CIL), a protocol-oriented overlay architecture positioned above conventional network transport and below autonomous AI applications. CIL introduces the Reasoning Exchange Protocol (REP) to route structured decision envelopes containing reasoning metadata rather than raw payloads. To resolve real-world deployment trade-offs, the framework integrates Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) for privacy-preserving verification and a Tiered Execution Architecture to isolate highthroughput edge transactions from deep asynchronous multi-agent consensus validation.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6956178\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "98e0a7fd65a191137f60862339bb8af1f2cbcbfac4137e48291703a65a590b2d", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "assumption_challenge", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.6759126", "doi:10.65109/lmxo2289", "doi:10.65109/gmqn5969", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6956178"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6759126", "https://doi.org/10.65109/lmxo2289", "https://doi.org/10.65109/gmqn5969", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6956178"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
